Specialist accuracy
Built for the task that general LLMs have to be talked into doing.

Arabic tashkeel is a precision layer, not an open-ended writing task. Large 30B-class local models and even SOTA hosted LLMs can reason about Arabic, but when the job is to vocalize existing text, Sukoon is the better fit: it is trained to preserve the original words, punctuation, and sentence order while adding the missing harakat. On the filtered benchmark it reaches 99.29% DER quality and 97.00% WER quality across 113,955 evaluated words.

That kind of predictable vocalization can push Arabic TTS into a new era: clearer pronunciation, better endings, shadda, tanween, pause handling, and more natural speech without a huge generative model in the loop. It also matters for education, from children learning to read to non-native learners studying Arabic, because the text stays the same while pronunciation support becomes visible. LLM prompts can hallucinate, paraphrase, normalize spelling, drop punctuation, or slowly drift when asked to process a full book, paper, or long document; Sukoon keeps the contract narrow and repeatable.

Repeatability is the product feature.
Same input, same contract, no surprise rewrites.

LLMs are generative systems. Even the best ones can hallucinate, paraphrase, change words, shift sentence structure, drop punctuation, or answer differently when you ask the same question again. That variability is useful for brainstorming, but it is an architectural mismatch for tashkeel, where the source text must remain the source text.

Sukoon is built around a preservation-first contract: keep the input words and sentence order, add the vocalization layer, and make the run repeatable. That matters when processing a book, lesson, paper, script, or production TTS corpus, because one changed word can change meaning and one drifting paragraph can break the trust of the whole pipeline.

Text preservedStable rerunsLong-form safe
Designed with clear scope boundaries.
Sukoon is a tashkeel specialist, not a general Arabic correction engine.
Tashkeel, not hamza correctionSukoon adds vocalization marks. It is not designed to fix hamza spelling or rewrite the base Arabic text.
Punctuation mattersSukoon works best with punctuated text because punctuation changes meaning, pause, and flow. Without it, the model is forced toward guessing intent.
Tanween is in scopeSukoon handles tanween, but exact fathatan placement, especially around alif, has orthographic disagreement across sources and styles.
Performance and cost

A tiny encoder pass instead of expensive autoregressive generation.

Sukoon is measured in words per second, not slow token-by-token generation. It is positioned as a specialist utility for high-volume Arabic preprocessing.

A specialist, not a generalist
Why purpose-built beats prompted every time.

Sukoon does not compete with large language models — it renders them irrelevant for this task. Rather than prompting a generative system and hoping it diacritizes faithfully, Sukoon is a custom encoder model built from the ground up with a single purpose: outperform every other model on Arabic diacritization. That focus translates directly into state-of-the-art accuracy — 99.29% DER and 97.00% WER — numbers no general-purpose LLM delivers at this cost, speed, or scale.

Because it is a deterministic pipeline rather than a generative model, Sukoon integrates into any existing workflow without the weight that comes with an LLM. No GPU cluster required, no multi-second inference rounds, no unpredictable outputs. With inference at < 2 ms per sentence, it slots into a production system as quietly as a logging call — barely measurable overhead, immediate results.

Cost is where the gap becomes a landslide. Running Sukoon is orders of magnitude cheaper than routing text through a cloud LLM API. This is what makes it genuinely different: not just a better model, but a different philosophy. AI as a real specialized tool that solves one problem as close to perfectly as possible, rather than a general system approximating many things adequately. That is the direction high-quality production AI is heading.

Our Message

AI is a tool —

arguably the most powerful one we've ever built.

We believe in creating things that are honest about what they are and genuinely useful where they are deployed. Our goal is to build technology designed to make people's lives better — not just to impress investors or fill out a pitch deck.

We don't see AI as a replacement for human beings; we see it as an extension of human ingenuity. Every great leap in civilization — the printing press, electricity, the internet — was powered by tools that expanded what we could do. AI is simply the next step. When used right, it has the potential to improve our quality of life in ways that actually matter: in medicine, education, culture, and the preservation of language and heritage. That potential is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

That's exactly why we're so skeptical of how AI is often treated today.

It's not a marketing gimmick. It's not a magic lever to inflate a stock price. It shouldn't be shoehorned into products where it adds zero value, or tossed around as a buzzword just to sound modern. AI is a technology with real consequences, and consequence demands honesty about where it actually helps and where it doesn't. Hype isn't a strategy; it's a waste of a pivotal moment.

We want to create AI that solves real problems — tools that integrate quietly into the way people already work, rather than demanding to replace them entirely. We focus on making things that are measurably better at a specific task than anything else out there.

Ultimately, we want to put capability directly into human hands.

Not AI that threatens —
AI that empowers.
